newsitem.title: USA: Mars Pathfinder mission a triumph beyond dreams.
newsitem.headline: Mars Pathfinder mission a triumph beyond dreams.

text.p: "Beyond my wildest dreams" has become the catch-phrase of space scientists as the Mars Pathfinder mission sends back a wealth of data from the Red Planet that even the scientists had not dared hope for.
Pathfinder and its "little engine that could," the Sojourner Rover, have told scientists about a huge flood that covered the Ares Vallis basin, the site of the landing, about 4-1/2 billion years ago.
The rover revealed the mineral composition of rocks that show Mars and Earth are probably "solar twins" in the way they were formed, and it has given the public vast, panoramic pictures to gasp over.
"This mission has rewritten the history of Mars," said Deputy Project Director Brian Muirhead.

But when all the public relations excitement is over and the media contingent of more than 570 pack their bags and return to their offices all over the world on Friday night, the show will go on behind the scenes.
"There's a lot more to come," said Muirhead.

The mission, nominally set for one week for the rover and a month for the lander craft, is expected to go on for several more weeks for the little Mars buggy and months more for the lander, with its stereo camera continuing to send back images and other data. "As long as they stay healthy we'll keep them active," Muirhead said.
With so many achievements and so many firsts, Muirhead, in an interview with Reuters, found it hard to come up with one main milestone for the mission, but settled on the landing.
"That would have to be my milestone. Before you can do all these things you have to put a spacecraft on Mars," he said.

Muirhead took particular pride in the landing, he said, because, "I WAS the spacecraft," explaining that as Flight Systems Manager in addition to deputy project manager he was responsible for the design and operation of Pathfinder and setting it down on Mars.

Muirhead said he believed the success of the Pathfinder mission could be the first step on the way to a manned expedition to Mars, adding that the lessons learned from Pathfinder would be extremely useful for a manned flight.
"I think we've shown that you can use innovative technology that hasn't been proved in space before, providing you test it thoroughly on Earth, taking every contingency into account," he said.
"The question is; how much risk is mankind willing to take to send a manned mission to Mars?"
One of the happiest people in a hysterically happy Pathfinder crew was Project Scientist Matthew Golombek, a geologist who has literally salivated over the results of the mission so far.

"I use the phrase 'beyond my wildest dreams' because it's the most accurate statement I can think of," he said. "I mean, who could ever have imagined that things would go so smoothly and so perfectly and that we would find out so much about Mars in such a short space of time."
But while the space scientists were euphoric, once the public had finished admiring the dramatic pictures sent from Mars, some started asking what had really been accomplished, and at what cost.

Mission Manager Richard Cook said he believed the public had got a lot of value out of the project over the last seven days. "We have shown we are a great nation and we are still in a position to achieve a technical marvel like this," he said.

Muirhead said the Pathfinder project had been an inspiration to all people, but particularly children. It had inspired classroom exercises in space exploration and hopefully inspired a generation of future scientsts, he added.

Mars is the focus of an ambitious eight-year exploration plan by NASA. The Mars Global Explorer, an orbiting spacecraft, is on its way to the Red Planet and will start mapping it later this year. Another orbiter will be launched in December 1998, followed by the lauch of a second lander, the Mars Surveyor, in 1999.

The Surveyor will not carry a rover and its landing will be guided by retro-rockets, not cushioned by airbags, as was the case with the Pathfinder. Surveyor will land near Mars' south pole and look for water.

In 2001 an orbiter and lander, complete with a rover about four times the size of Sojourner, will be sent to Mars. With an eye to an eventual manned expedition, Surveyor 01 will carry out an experiment to try to generate rocket propellant from material at the landing site.

Two more orbiters and landers with rovers will be launched in 2003 and 2005, culminating in the most ambitious project, the 2005 mission, which will return samples to Earth collected earlier by either the 2001 or the 2003 Surveyors.
